scenes.narration: Code is read far more often than it is written. So this array language puts the meaning where your eye already is, in how each name looks. Here is how to read it, one idea at a time, from its syntax poster.

scenes.narration: Start with the first letter. When it is underlined, the name is a function, like reverse. With no underline, the name is a value, a number, a list, or a table.

scenes.narration: A small letter above the name says where it came from. One mark for your own program, another for a library's export, another for a helper that only this file can see. So you never hunt for a definition.

scenes.narration: Importing a library gives it a short name of your choosing. That name then shows above every word you use from it, so a reader knows which import to open.

scenes.narration: The left arrow binds a name, to a value or to a function. But the equals sign never binds. It only compares, and gives ones and zeros.

scenes.narration: Write a function next to a value, and it applies to it. Put a quote in front of a function, and you pass the function itself, as a value, to another function. That is how each and reduce get their work.

scenes.narration: A small number below a function attaches an axis to it. Reduce sums down the first axis by default. With a two below it, it sums along the second axis instead.

scenes.narration: The same mark works for rotate and transpose. Rotate along axis two shifts every row. Transpose with no axis reverses them all, so rows become columns.

scenes.narration: A small number above a value is a power, so x squared looks the way it does on paper. Above a function, it applies the function that many times. Life to the fourth runs four generations, and the glider moves.
